Concept Paper · First Draft · 2026

The Canvas
is the Message

A concept for reassessing the picture support in contemporary art. The canvas — understood as carrier, material, object, and context — is itself a statement. Not background. Not a tool. An actor.

Read the Concept
Scroll

Canvas

I

Starting Point

In 1964, Marshall McLuhan coined the phrase “The medium is the message.” He meant that the transmitting medium — television, radio, print — carries a message of its own, independent of its actual content. Television shapes differently than radio, radio differently than print.

This concept transfers that idea to pictorial space: the canvas — understood as carrier, material, object, and context — is itself a statement.

“The Canvas is the Message” — the picture support is not a neutral surface but a meaning-bearing element that shapes, comments on, undermines, or reinforces the content.
II

A Global Given

The unity of canvas and meaning is not an avant-garde concept. It is the historical default state of human image-making — worldwide, for millennia. The idea of the neutral picture support is the historical exception, not the rule. It emerged with the commodification of art in the Western bohemian tradition of the 19th century, when art became a tradable good and the canvas shrank to a standardized, interchangeable surface.

Before art became a market commodity, the canvas was never neutral. It was body, bone, stone, bark — always already meaning-bearing.

Indigenous and Pre-Modern Art Worldwide

Arctic

Walrus Ivory and Bone

The carved walrus tusk already carries the relationship between human, animal, and spirit within it. Canvas and content are the same event.

Australia

Aboriginal Bark Painting

The bark connects to land, origin, and law. Dreamtime painting is meaningless without the material's provenance.

Pacific Northwest Coast

Totem Poles

The cedar trunk is itself an ancestor, not merely wood. The figures are drawn out of it, not applied onto it.

Paleolithic

Cave Painting

The cave itself is a canvas with a spiritual topography. Animals are painted where their energy resides — ledges, cracks, depths.

Mesoamerica

Ceramics and Codices

Clay from the place, shaped for function, painted with genealogy. The codex carries the world before it is inscribed.

Africa & Oceania

Body Painting, Textiles

The living body as canvas. Weaving patterns as genealogy, law, identity — not decoration.

East Asia

Bone Flutes, Ritual Objects

The material sounds before it is shaped. The canvas is carrier and instrument at once.

Japan

Water Calligraphy, Ukiyo-e

Impermanence as statement. The disappearance of water calligraphy is part of the work itself.

The Interruption

With the rise of the art market in the 18th and 19th centuries, the canvas was standardized and thereby seemingly neutralized. The canvas became a trade format. This concept is therefore not a new invention. It is a reclamation.

Revival in Contemporary Culture

Graffiti

On trains, walls, wrecked cars: the canvas carries history, legality, risk. The choice of location is the statement.

Banksy — Stolen Wall

When a wall painted by Banksy was removed and auctioned off, the canvas was worth more than any painting on neutral canvas.

Recontextualization

Mickey Mouse turns subversive with Crumb, political with Banksy, commodity with Murakami. The more recognizable the canvas, the greater the friction.

Ai Weiwei — Han Vases

A 2,000-year-old vase, coated in industrial paint. Canvas fights canvas — tradition against modernity.

Tattoo Art

The body as a living canvas — it breathes, ages, changes. A co-author over time. And it dies with the work.

Garden Art

The canvas actively grows, with or against intention. The same bed yields a different picture in April, June, October.

Snow, Sand, Ice

The canvas determines the work's lifespan from the outset. Impermanence is not a limitation but a statement.

Supreme on a Brick

The brand name ennobles the mundane — or exposes itself. The canvas comments on the value of what's printed on it.

Whatever looks valuable gets copied fast: already sold as a knockoff building brick on Indian B2B marketplaces.

A curated selection from a longer list of contemporary examples in the full concept paper.

III

The Attribute Model

At the core of the concept is a multidimensional attribute system that makes every work describable and comparable in terms of its relationship to its canvas.

01MaterialityPhysical / digital / immaterial / ephemeral
02Social Status of the CanvasPrestigious ↔ mundane ↔ taboo ↔ neutral
03Prior History of the CanvasUntouched / already inscribed / serial / collectively used
04ScaleStamp ↔ wall ↔ landscape ↔ city
05Canvas–Content RelationshipHarmonious / ironic / subversive / reinforcing
06ControllabilityCan the artist control the canvas? (Water on stone: no)
07Edition / ReproducibilityOne-of-a-kind / limited edition / series / unlimited
08PermanenceFrom eternal (marble, pyramid) to fleeting (water, body, air)
09Authorship of the CanvasAnonymous / historically charged / prominent / collective
10SellabilityCan the work be separated from its canvas? (Train graffiti: barely — as long as the wagon is still running. German rapper Sammy Deluxe put a retired subway car in his garden just to have one to paint.)

The Tension Matrix

The relationship between canvas quality and content produces four fundamental fields of meaning. Not a value judgment — a descriptive and conceptual tool.

High-Value ContentNeutral ContentLow-Value Content
Premium CanvasExpectation confirmedQuiet ironySubversion / provocation
Everyday ObjectDemocratizationConceptual neutralityNihilism / purity
Ephemeral CanvasTragedy / memento moriZen / process artDissolution
Taboo ObjectShock + meaningPolitical statementNihilism
IV

Scholarly Context and the Gap

Related positions exist, but each addresses only partial aspects:

Supports/Surfaces (France, ~1969) — deconstruction of the canvas as material, within painting.
Daniel Buren — use of urban space as canvas, primarily as institutional critique.
Julia Townsend (2025) — the choice of canvas as a poetic act: an essay, not an analytical framework.
Ai Weiwei (Colored Vases, from 2006) — close to the concept, but without an analytical model.
What's missing: A systematic, comparative model — already implemented in an early form as a spiderweb comparison (Canvas Comparator). What's still open is the final data structure: a robust system for consistently evaluating canvas meaning across all materialities, cultures, and contexts. A rough estimate is already possible; refinement is the next step.
V

Exhibition Concept

The exhibition realizes the concept not as theory but as a sensorially experienced juxtaposition — original and selected reference works that exemplify the dimensions of the attribute model.

Work Series

Stamp Series

Same motif, different stamp series as canvas. Postmark, engraving, print run as conceptual variables.

Work Series

Canvas Degradation

A high-value motif on a plastic bag. A banal motif on handmade deckle-edged paper.

Work Series

Ephemeral Intervention

A water-based work on a wall or on stone, within the exhibition space itself.

Work Series

Serial Canvas

Work on a newspaper page, record sleeve, magazine cover — the informational context of the carrier remains legible.

Work Series

Collective Canvas

An already used, inscribed object becomes the basis — what came before remains visible.

Catalog

The catalog is itself a canvas: it doesn't just document the works but exposes the attribute model as an intellectual scaffold — with essays, illustrations, and a visual index of the canvas attributes of every work shown.

VI

The Canvas of the Future

Three developments pose new, open questions for the attribute model — and make it more urgent at the same time.

Kinetic & Immersive Art

Artists like Olafur Eliasson have radically expanded the canvas: light, water, temperature, atmosphere become material. The exhibition space is not a container for the work — it is the work.

Jean Tinguely anticipated this kinetically: machines that destroy themselves. The canvas as process, not object. Permanence — one of the ten dimensions — becomes a real-time variable.

Generative AI Art

Autonomous generative AI art challenges one of the model's basic categories: authorship. If the algorithm itself determines which canvas it works on — does “The Canvas is the Message” still hold?

Whose message is it then? The programmer's? The dataset's? The canvas's own, becoming meaning-bearing without human mediation?

What remains of artistic intention when the canvas has long since become more meaningful than the act taking place on it?
VII

Next Steps

Realize first exemplary works that make the attribute model visible.

Prepare an expanded version of the concept paper for contact with Kunsthalle Bielefeld.

Draft the accompanying essay: theoretical background, references, scope.

Deliberate Exclusions

This concept focuses on the visible, material canvas. Deliberately set aside, but explicitly acknowledged as its own territory:

Theater — the stage as canvas Performance Art — the body without an object Photography & Film — negative, paper, format Literature & Poetry — book vs. pamphlet Music — instrument as canvas

These fields are definitely worth examining through the same lens — they are set aside here to sharpen the focus, not because they fall outside the concept.

Message

The real work lies in observing: once you start reading the canvas as a bearer of meaning, you see it everywhere — on the street, in the museum, online, in everyday life. The model is a playing field. The attributes are tools. What gets played with them remains open.

This concept makes no claim to completeness. The ten attributes are a beginning, not a boundary. The examples are invitations, not an inventory.
